extracted.intended_audience: historians, philosophers, and educated readers evaluating religious claims and historical evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methods for assessing the credibility of miraculous and supernatural claims in historical sources, and for explaining the historical rise and decline of belief in miracles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent possibility of miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no contradiction involved in the belief that spiritual beings of power and wisdom exceeding our own might exist and, existing, might perform feats surpassing human understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss a reported miracle merely because it seems extraordinary; first ask whether the event is logically possible (the author notes some classes of miracles are 'perfectly free from logical difficulty'). If antecedent possibility holds, further enquiry into evidence and context is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and amount of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual sceptical objection is that miracles lack sufficient evidence; however, many minor historical facts are authenticated by far less evidence than some alleged miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the quantity and quality of testimony for the miracle to that routinely accepted for other historical facts (examples given: Stigmata of St. Francis, miracle of the holy thorn, accounts by Tacitus and Suetonius). Evaluate whether the evidence would suffice for an ordinary historical fact and whether special objections apply to the supernatural claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal predisposition toward the miraculous
rubrics_metrics.description: The predisposition of men in certain stages of society towards the miraculous is of capital importance: in some periods miraculous stories are 'invariably circulated and credited,' making ordinary amounts of evidence inadequate for a supernatural claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the social and intellectual conditions (education, imagination, personification tendencies) that make a population prone to produce and accept miraculous narratives; where such predisposition is strong, much greater critical caution is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of historic development as explanatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of certain beliefs (e.g., fairies, dæmons) is best resolved by observing the laws of historic development—beliefs appear in certain stages and decline with education; 'the question ... has not been resolved by an examination of evidence, but by an observation of the laws of historic development.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative historical patterns (presence of legends in ignorant/rustic populations and their decline with education) to infer whether a belief is the normal product of a mental stage rather than a trace of actual supernatural events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive method: examine hits and misses
rubrics_metrics.description: An inductive enquirer must 'examine not only the facts that corroborate our theory, but also those which oppose it'—avoid collecting only confirming examples ('men “mark the hits, but not the misses”').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct a comprehensive survey that counts both corroborating and countervailing instances (e.g., successful and unsuccessful prayers for rain, epidemics in orthodox and heterodox regions) to avoid selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity or persistence beyond natural explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: We should 'examine whether events have tended in a given direction with a uniformity or a persistence that is not naturally explicable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a series of events shows sustained, systematic deviation from natural probabilities (not just occasional coincidences), infer a special cause only after ruling out natural explanations and chance; use broad historical sampling to test persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental detectability of alleged forces
rubrics_metrics.description: If an influence more powerful than military agency is said to direct events (e.g., battles), 'the action of this force must be detected as we would detect electricity, or any other force, by experiment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand empirical, repeatable tests or observable, measurable effects for claims that posit operative forces; treat claims that cannot in principle be tested with correspondingly greater scepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical consistency for institutional infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim that a Church or institution is infallible, one should 'examine, by a wide and careful survey of ecclesiastical history, whether this Church has actually been immutable and consistent in its teaching.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess councils, convocations, and institutional decisions for harmony, wisdom, and resistance to error over time; check whether the institution has supported views later shown false or blocked intellectual progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress of physical science and the reign of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The progress of physical science 'reveals the reign of law' and shows that many phenomena once attributed to spiritual agency have natural causes, reducing the need to invoke miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether scientific explanations remove the mystery (examples: comets, disease, epilepsy, nightmare). The more phenomena admit natural, law-governed explanations, the less plausible claims of special divine intervention become.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three chief causes of decline in miraculous narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual decadence of miraculous narratives accompanies advancing civilisation and is chiefly traced to: (1) greater accuracy of observation and statement, (2) increased power of abstraction, and (3) progress of physical science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining historical decline in belief, weigh these three factors as primary mechanisms rather than assuming wholesale falsification or conspiracy; use them to interpret changes in reportage and belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test claims by comparative historical correlation (example: plagues vs vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that plagues or pestilences are sent as punishment must be 'tested by a comprehensive examination of the history of plagues ... and of periods of great vice and heterodoxy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic, comparative historical data to test causal claims linking moral states to events; look for counterexamples, geographical patterns, and alternative explanations (e.g., environmental causes, contagion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware selection bias and testimonial survivorship
rubrics_metrics.description: People 'mark the hits, but not the misses' — votive tablets of those who escaped are preserved, while the shipwrecked are forgotten; successful outcomes are emphasised and failures omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust for survivorship and reporting biases when evaluating testimonial collections; ask how many unsuccessful cases were omitted and whether publicity or ritual mechanisms selectively preserved confirming accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek proximate natural explanations for particular legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Many legends have proximate natural causes (examples: epilepsy, nightmare, forms of madness leading to accounts of demoniacal possession, incubus, lycanthropy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before inferring supernatural agency, test specific physiological or environmental explanations relevant to the case; where a plausible natural mechanism fits the particulars, it reduces the need to posit the miraculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probabilistic reasoning and limits to variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent miracles that are simply improbable coincidences must be judged by probability limits—if improbable results recur uniformly (dice always showing same number, repeatedly victorious disadvantaged armies), we should infer a special cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply probabilistic thinking: check whether repeated patterns exceed reasonable chance given underlying conditions; distinguish occasional unlikely coincidences from systematic improbabilities requiring explanation.
